# Barycentric coordinate counts: a convex-body obstruction and a simplex theorem

Let d>=1, N=d+1, and let B be a d-dimensional simplex with barycentric
coordinates lambda_1,...,lambda_N. For a convex body D subset B define

    k=#{i:sup_D lambda_i>1/N},       r=N-k.

The proposed implication

    |D|>=2^(-d)|B|  ==>  k>=gamma_d N/2                 (1)

is false for general convex D. It is true, with the stronger conclusion
k>=N/2, when D is itself a d-simplex. Both assertions below are exact.
They are auxiliary geometric statements and imply no OC counterexample.

## 1. The maximal body for a fixed set of excluded coordinates

If r coordinates have supremum at most 1/N, then D is contained in

    P_(N,r)={x in B:lambda_i(x)<=1/N for i=1,...,r},

after relabeling. Conversely this truncated simplex realizes the largest
volume under precisely those upper constraints. For d>=1 its normalized
volume is

    |P_(N,r)|/|B|
       =sum_(j=0)^r (-1)^j binom(r,j)(1-j/N)^d.         (2)

Indeed inclusion-exclusion applies to the r violations lambda_i>1/N.
For a fixed j-element subset of violations, shifting those barycentric
coordinates down by 1/N leaves a simplex of total barycentric mass
1-j/N. Its normalized volume is (1-j/N)^d. Changing weak to strict
inequalities affects only finitely many hyperplanes of zero d-volume.
If j=N the surviving set is at most one point, and the factor is zero;
there is no 0^0 because d>=1.

If k>=1, P_(N,r) is full-dimensional. Its constrained coordinate suprema
are exactly 1/N: choose that coordinate equal to 1/N and put all the
remaining mass into a free coordinate. Each free coordinate has supremum
one because its vertex of B belongs to P_(N,r). Thus its count really
is k, with the strict inequality convention in the definition.

For later comparison, its volume also has the integral representation

    |P_(N,r)|/|B|
      =d!/(k-1)! integral_[0,1/N]^r
                               (1-sum_i x_i)^(k-1) dx. (3)

Choose one free barycentric coordinate as the dependent coordinate.
For fixed r constrained coordinates the remaining k-1 coordinates fill
a simplex of volume (1-sum x)^(k-1)/(k-1)!. Dividing by the volume
1/d! of the full standard simplex gives (3). The entire cube is allowed
because sum x<=r/N<1. Affine changes from the standard simplex multiply
the numerator and denominator by the same Jacobian.

## 2. A small exact general-body counterexample

Take d=15, N=16, r=13, k=3, and D=P_(16,13). Formula (2) gives

    |D|/|B|=29158754625/562949953421312,

and hence

    |D|/|B|-2^(-15)
       =11978885441/562949953421312>0.                 (4)

But

    gamma_15*16/2-3
       =5548326153291759/144115188075855872>0.          (5)

Every one of the thirteen constrained coordinate suprema equals 1/16,
and each of the three free coordinate suprema equals one. Thus (4)--(5)
contradict (1) with no strict/weak ambiguity. This D is full-dimensional:
one interior point has its thirteen constrained coordinates equal to
1/32 and its three free coordinates equal to 19/96.

## 3. An independently checked Jensen certificate

There is also an exact example at d=30, N=31, r=26, k=5 that does not
require evaluating the alternating sum. Let X_i be independent uniform
variables on [0,1/31]. Then (3) and convexity of t^4 give

    |P_(31,26)|/|B|
      =30!/(4!31^26) E[(1-sum_i X_i)^4]
      >=30!/(4!31^26) (18/31)^4
       =30!*18^4/(4!*31^30)>2^(-30).                  (6)

The last inequality is verified by the exact ratio

    2^30*30!*18^4/(4!*31^30)
      =1245772453542801712398066946425728532480000000
        /550618520345910837374536871905139185678862401>1.

The count also fails strictly:

    gamma_30*31/2-5
      =14136127281855010100881149692719486180828645
        /17761887753093897979823770061456102763834271>0.

This is a second certificate, not an asymptotic argument.

## 4. A determinant bound when D is a simplex

Suppose now that D is a d-dimensional simplex, with vertices
w_1,...,w_N. Form its barycentric vertex matrix

    V_ij=lambda_i(w_j).

Every entry is nonnegative and every column sums to one. Moreover,

    |D|/|B|=|det V|.                                  (7)

To see (7), replace the last row by the sum of all rows, which becomes
the all-ones row. Subtract the last column from the others and expand
along the last row. The remaining determinant is the usual edge-vector
determinant in d independent barycentric coordinates. Both D and B use
the same affine coordinate Jacobian and the same factor 1/d!, proving
the ratio formula.

If k=0, every point of D would have all N barycentric coordinates at
most 1/N. Their sum being one forces every coordinate to equal 1/N,
so D would be a singleton. Thus k>=1 for a positive-volume simplex.

Choose one of the k free rows. Add every other row to it, converting
it to the all-ones row. This operation preserves the determinant.
From each of the r constrained rows subtract 1/(2N) times that row
of ones. From each of the other k-1 free rows subtract one half times
the row of ones. These row operations also preserve the determinant.

Each constrained row now has all entries in [-1/(2N),1/(2N)], so its
Euclidean norm is at most 1/(2 sqrt(N)). Each remaining free row has
entries in [-1/2,1/2], so its norm is at most sqrt(N)/2. The ones row
has norm sqrt(N). Hadamard's inequality therefore gives the exact bound

    |D|/|B|=|det V|
       <=(1/(2 sqrt(N)))^r (sqrt(N)/2)^(k-1) sqrt(N)
        =N^(k-N/2)/2^(N-1).                           (8)

Hadamard follows, for example, by applying Gram--Schmidt to the rows:
the absolute determinant is the product of the successive perpendicular
component lengths, each no greater than the original row norm. Thus no
unproved maximal-determinant classification is involved in (8).

If |D|/|B|>=2^(-(N-1)), (8) implies N^(k-N/2)>=1. Since N>=2,

    k>=N/2.                                          (9)

Finally gamma_d<1 for d>=1, so (9) implies the proposed weaker count
k>=gamma_d N/2. The hypothesis that D itself is a simplex is essential:
the truncated-simplex bodies in sections 2--3 violate the weaker count.

## 5. Zero-dimensional convention and scope

If d=0 is allowed in the proposed coordinate-count statement, it fails
even for a simplex: B=D is the singleton, its only barycentric coordinate
equals one, k=0, and gamma_0 N/2=1/2. The positive-dimensional theorem
therefore explicitly assumes d>=1. This has no bearing on the original
d=0 mixed-integer depth statement, whose structure is different.

The general-body counterexamples do not have simplex shape, and their
ordinary depth need not equal the simplex constant. Conversely the
simplex count controls only the listed barycentric facet directions.
Neither result alone supplies an ambient halfspace-depth theorem.

The later note `candidate 986ab1688d049a3b`
retains actual row maxima in the centered-row Hadamard argument. It gives
an explicit positive margin above 1/N on at least ceil(N/2) coordinates,
and converts that pointwise margin into an integrated bound for actual
minimized endpoint-pair cap costs of compatible three-fiber bodies.
